source.title: Harmless interpolation of noisy data in regression
source.authors: Vidya K. Muthukumar; Kailas Vodrahalli; Anant Sahai

record.file_problem: Full text supplied; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes noisy overparameterized linear regression and explicitly says its conclusions do not settle generalization in deep neural networks; it also qualifies harmless interpolation by feature family, estimator, and signal/noise conditions.
record.gate_note: The paper tests interpolation and generalization in linear regression, not the neural-network random-label/natural-label coexistence claim. Its neural-network statements in the introduction and conclusion are background or explicit limitations, not experimental results. Rows below cover the paper's own reported linear-regression results that bear on interpolation and the overparameterized generalization premise; cited results from other studies are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study's own theory and simulations concern noisy linear regression with fixed features. None measures the neural-network systems or mechanisms named in V1–V8. Increasing linear feature count is related to V2 but does not test widening trained ReLU networks. Neural-network findings and optimizer comparisons appear as cited background; Section 6.1 explicitly leaves their generalization unresolved.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. Add the authors' practical qualification: in their correctly specified linear setting, optimal denoising is preferable to interpolation, whose extra noise-fitting cost can vanish under extreme overparameterization. Minimum-norm fitting can dissipate signal; parsimonious fitting absorbs noise poorly; hybrid constructions balance these goals. The authors explicitly leave deep-network generalization unresolved.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies theoretical and empirical overparameterized linear regression with continuous noisy targets, not neural networks trained on natural labels or fixed random labels. It analyzes ideal interpolation, minimum-norm, sparse, weighted, and hybrid interpolators.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature family and whitening, training-point sampling pattern, feature count relative to sample count, signal sparsity and representation, noise variance, and feature weights affect the reported generalization behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: For Gaussian features, the ideal linear interpolator's excess test MSE scales as σ²n/d under extreme overparameterization. Simulations compare this price across feature families and sampling patterns.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Noise interpolation can have vanishing excess prediction cost in linear regression under suitable feature and overparameterization conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Minimum-norm regression shows double descent for constant-aligned Gaussian features, but approaches null risk for isotropic sparse signals. Feature weighting changes signal preservation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generalization from additional linear features depends on signal alignment and the estimator's feature weighting.

fits_no_version.finding: Parsimonious interpolators fit noise less efficiently than the ideal interpolator; hybrid sparse-estimation and minimum-norm procedures achieve favorable theoretical rates and illustrative simulation performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse signal preservation and harmless noise interpolation require different estimator properties in noisy linear regression.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory (ISIT 2019)
record.problems: The experiments are primarily illustrative simulations with some settings using small n; many plotted values are not given numerically in prose. Ideal interpolation requires knowledge of the true signal and is not implementable. Results concern linear regression, and the authors explicitly leave deep neural networks unresolved.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Cited prior-study results and neural-network background statements were excluded; figure-only values were not estimated.

untested.parts: Neural-network fitting of random versus natural labels and their corresponding held-out classification accuracies.
Test error as trained ReLU networks widen beyond zero training error; linear feature-count sweeps do not measure this.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning on the named benchmark types.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects and their dependence on data size, dropout strength and augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps and comparisons with other generalization measures.
Retraining after removing memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because no row measures a listed version; this does not negate the reported linear-regression findings. The study is not an original source for these versions, but no verdict labels are warranted because it tests none of them.

versions.untested_parts: Neural networks fitting fixed random labels and generalizing on natural labels; no classification experiment.
No sweep of one-hidden-layer ReLU network width past the interpolation threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier comparison.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparison.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or generalization-measure comparison.
No removal or retraining of memorized examples.

rows.subject: ideal interpolator
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical lower bound and achievable upper bound on excess test MSE as feature count grows for Gaussian features.

conditions.value: d > n, especially d much greater than n

rows.measure: Expected test MSE minus irreducible noise error
rows.value: For Gaussian features, lower and upper bounds scale as σ²n/d (up to constants) in the heavily overparameterized regime; the bound tends to zero as d grows.
rows.uncertainty: High-probability bounds are stated in Corollaries 1 and 2; exact probability depends on δ and n.
rows.note: This is a theoretical ideal interpolator requiring knowledge of the true signal, not a practical training recipe.
rows.check: The Gaussian ideal-interpolator bounds concern excess regression MSE, not any listed version. The stated asymptotic scaling is supported for sufficiently large d/n; vanishing error requires n/d to approach zero.

rows.subject: minimum-ℓ2-norm interpolator
rows.operation_detail: Vary number of Gaussian features for a constant signal plus noise.

conditions.value: iid Gaussian features distributed as N(1, 0.01)
constant 1, not exactly representable at any finite d

rows.value: The text describes a clear double-descent behavior and says test MSE decreases with increased overparameterization.
rows.note: The numerical curve is figure-only; the row records only the qualitative description in the text.
rows.check: The double descent result is for linear minimum-norm regression with added Gaussian features, not neural-network width in V2. The paper defines test MSE here as excluding irreducible noise.

rows.subject: minimum-ℓ2-norm interpolator
rows.size_stated: d features; n = 5000; signal sparsity k = 500
rows.operation_detail: Vary feature count for a sparse signal under iid standard Gaussian features.
rows.baseline: Test error from using α = 0 (null risk)
rows.value: Test MSE converges to the same level as the test error from α = 0 as d increases.
rows.note: The text describes the trend; precise values appear in a figure.
rows.check: Convergence to null risk concerns linear regression and cannot establish a partial effect on any listed version. Figure 7 includes three noise variances; the row's σ² = 0.01 condition selects only one.

rows.subject: minimum-ℓ2-norm interpolator
rows.size_stated: n = 15; number of features d varied
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate the ideal interpolation price as feature count grows across feature families and sampling schemes.

conditions.value: regularly spaced or random, depending on feature family

rows.baseline: Noise level and interpolation threshold are plotted as references
rows.value: Text says all curves are similar when d/n ≥ 10; regularly spaced Fourier features achieve the Θ(σ²n/d) scaling for large d.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 2(b) shows error bars, but numerical values are not stated.
rows.note: Plots show medians; figure-only numerical values are not reconstructed.
rows.check: Correct the subject to ideal interpolator: Figure 2 plots the fundamental price of interpolation, not general minimum-ℓ2 signal fitting. Its feature-family comparisons do not test any listed version.

rows.subject: minimum-ℓ2-norm interpolator
rows.operation_detail: Inspect recovered signal coefficients under iid Gaussian features.
rows.value: The text states signal bleeds into spurious features, lowering survival in true features and increasing contamination by spurious features.
rows.note: Qualitative result; coefficient values are shown in a figure only.
rows.check: Signal-coefficient bleed in linear regression is outside V1–V8. Figure 4(b) specifies d = 30000, which should be added to the condition.

rows.subject: minimum-weighted-ℓ2-norm interpolator
rows.operation_detail: Change feature weights to impose strong, medium, or weak prior weight on low-frequency Fourier features.

conditions.value: strong, medium, or weak low-frequency weighting

rows.value: The learned function approximates the true signal well with a strong prior on low-frequency features, and suffers signal bleed as the prior weakens.
rows.note: Separate strong, medium, and weak settings are pictured, but the supplied prose gives a qualitative comparison rather than values per setting.
rows.check: Figure 5 qualitatively compares learned functions under feature weighting; it does not report numerical test MSE or test a listed version. Split strong, medium and weak priors if retaining separate condition rows.

rows.subject: minimum-ℓ2-norm interpolator
rows.operation_detail: Compare OMP to completion, basis pursuit, minimum-ℓ2 interpolation, hybrid OMP, hybrid Lasso, ideal interpolation, and zero fit on noisy sparse linear data.
rows.baseline: Ideal interpolator and zero-fit are plotted as references
rows.value: Figures show results across three noise variances; text says hybrid interpolators' test MSE closely track the ideal MSE for all these ranges.
rows.uncertainty: Figure-only numerical values; no error bars stated here.
rows.note: The claim about hybrid methods is included because it reports performance of interpolation methods on the claim's generalization subject; exact plotted values are not reconstructed.
rows.check: The value describes hybrid OMP and hybrid Lasso, so the subject should identify those methods rather than the minimum-ℓ2 interpolator. Split methods and noise conditions. This comparison of the study's interpolation procedures bears on no listed version.

rows.subject: OMP to completion
rows.size_stated: d features; n = 1000 or 50 in fixed-n plots
rows.operation_detail: Vary feature count and growth regime while fitting pure noise with OMP to completion.

conditions.value: fixed n=1000; fixed n=50; d=n²; d=eⁿ

rows.value: Text says OMP and BP test MSE decrease only slightly with n,d and extremely slowly and negligibly compared with ideal test MSE.
rows.note: Figure displays OMP, BP, and ideal curves; the prose reports the qualitative trend jointly.
rows.check: Pure-noise linear-regression MSE does not test any listed version. The four sample/feature growth regimes should be separate rows; a partial state cannot be transferred to neural-network width.

rows.subject: basis pursuit (minimum-ℓ1-norm interpolator)
rows.size_stated: d features; n = 1000 or 50 in fixed-n plots
rows.operation_detail: Vary feature count and growth regime while fitting pure noise with basis pursuit.

conditions.value: fixed n=1000; fixed n=50; d=n²; d=eⁿ

rows.value: Text says OMP and BP test MSE decrease only slightly with n,d and extremely slowly and negligibly compared with ideal test MSE.
rows.note: Figure displays OMP, BP, and ideal curves; the prose reports the qualitative trend jointly.
rows.check: Pure-noise basis-pursuit regression does not test any listed version. Separate the four growth regimes; their slow error decrease is not evidence about V2's neural networks.

rows.subject: β-parsimonious interpolating operator
rows.operation_detail: Prove a lower bound on test MSE for parsimonious interpolators on a constructed sparse-linear-model instance.

conditions.value: zero signal instance is used in proof

rows.value: Lower bound stated as βσ²(1−δ)/(C ln(d/n)); text says it is not harmless noise fitting and can decay only logarithmically when d=n^q.
rows.uncertainty: High-probability bounds; probabilities are specified in Theorem 2.
rows.locator: Theorem 2 and discussion immediately following, Section 5.1
rows.note: This challenges an assumption that overparameterization alone makes all interpolators harmless; the result concerns a broad class of parsimonious linear interpolators.
rows.check: The existential lower bound concerns parsimonious linear interpolators, not any listed version. It does not show reversed width effects: a slowly decaying lower bound does not establish increasing test error or rule out consistency.

rows.subject: hybrid interpolator using order-optimal first-step estimator
rows.operation_detail: First estimate sparse signal, then interpolate the residual with a minimum-norm correction.

conditions.value: first-step estimator order-optimal in estimation and prediction error

rows.baseline: Optimal interpolation and sparse signal recovery lower bounds
rows.value: Upper bound in Equation (31): C''σ² k ln(d/k)/n + C'''σ² n/(√d−2√n)² + σ²; authors call the hybrid order-optimal among interpolating solutions.
rows.uncertainty: High-probability conditions are referenced in Corollary 5; constants are not specified numerically.
rows.note: This is a theoretical construction, not a neural-network training result.
rows.check: The hybrid construction tests no listed version. Equation (31) is transcribed as printed, but its added σ² conflicts with Definition 1's excess-MSE convention; flag this source inconsistency when comparing bounds.

rows.subject: hybrid Lasso / hybrid OMP
rows.operation_detail: Use Lasso or OMP signal estimates in the first step, then interpolate residual.
rows.value: The text states a bound of C''σ²k ln(d)/n + C'''σ² + σ²n/d for either hybrid estimator.
rows.uncertainty: Constants universal; conditions are described in Appendix A.3.
rows.note: Corollary 7 uses square-root Lasso and does not require knowledge of σ²; the statement shares the same displayed form.
rows.check: Hybrid sparse-regression guarantees test no listed version. Separate Lasso, OMP and square-root-Lasso because their assumptions differ. The displayed bounds include an irreducible-noise term despite Definition 1's excess-MSE convention.

rows.subject: ideal interpolator on Legendre and Fourier features
rows.size_stated: n and d varied; 50 random draws
rows.operation_detail: Compare interpolation error near the threshold for regularly spaced versus randomly drawn training points.
rows.measure: Test MSE; mean and median with 85% confidence intervals
rows.value: Text says distributional assumptions make a significant difference: randomly drawn points have much lower minimum singular value, heavy-tailed behavior, and median test MSE higher than with regularly spaced points.
rows.note: The paper's prose directly states qualitative differences; plotted numerical values are not reconstructed.
rows.check: Sampling-pattern effects on linear interpolation test no listed version. Figure 9 includes ideal, minimum-ℓ2 and hybrid schemes; identify which curves support each result and separate feature families and sampling conditions.
